name: Tennessee

west.label: West Tennessee
climate: {county} County is part of the Western Grand Division defined in Tennessee Code Annotated section 4-1-204. NWS Memphis says June is the most active month for thunderstorm wind events in its warning area, and that the majority of those events occur between March and July. It says hail occurs most frequently from March through June, with May the most active month.

NWS Memphis studied tornadoes from 2007 to 2020 in its warning area and found that April accounted for 57 of 276 tornadoes, with May next at 50. The study reports that tornadoes occurred most frequently between 5:00 and 6:00 PM, with 40 of the 276 in that hour. It adds that tornado activity dramatically lowers from June through November. NWS Memphis also says severe weather reports peak in the late afternoon and early evening hours, and the Memphis warning area includes {county} County's region.

NOAA's Tennessee state climate summary says summers are warm and humid for most of the state, while winters are cool with occasional episodes of very cold arctic air. It states that total annual precipitation has been mostly above average since 1990. It describes summer average high temperatures as warmer in western and central Tennessee than in the eastern portion of the state. It adds that winter weather includes occasional snow and ice storms, a statewide statement that includes {county} County.

middle.label: Middle Tennessee
climate: {county} County is part of the Middle Grand Division defined in Tennessee Code Annotated section 4-1-203. NWS Nashville's tornado statistics page lists an average of 18 tornadoes per year in Middle Tennessee for 1995 to 2025, against 31 per year statewide. A separate NWS Nashville climatology covers Middle Tennessee tornadoes from 1830 to 2003, and a third NWS Nashville study covers heavy precipitation.

NWS Nashville's tornado climatology of Middle Tennessee for 1830 to 2003 says nearly two-thirds of its tornadoes occurred in March, April and May. It reports that the most common hour of the day is 5:00 to 5:59 PM Central Standard Time. For the same 1830 to 2003 record it notes a secondary peak centered around November, when thirty tornadoes, 6 percent of the total, struck, a note that applies to {county} County's region.

NWS Nashville's heavy precipitation climatology for Middle Tennessee, based on 1961 to 1990 data from 43 cooperative stations, calls November through May the wet season, when two-thirds of annual precipitation falls. It gives March as the wettest month at 5.76 inches and October as the driest at 3.38 inches. These are regional figures for the area that includes {county} County.

east.label: East Tennessee
climate: {county} County is part of the Eastern Grand Division defined in Tennessee Code Annotated section 4-1-202. NOAA's Tennessee state climate summary says temperatures decrease as elevation increases, averaging a 3 degree F decline per 1,000 feet. It describes the Cumberland Plateau as averaging 2,000 feet in elevation and Smoky Mountains peaks as reaching 6,000 feet, and it says these higher areas are cooler than lower-elevation areas.

NWS Morristown's snowfall records show how elevation matters in East Tennessee. For March 12 to 14, 1993, the office lists widespread 24 to 36 inch amounts in the mountains and 40 to 60 inches on the highest peaks of Sevier County. For February 12 to 14, 1960, it lists 10 to 15 inches in the mountains and 5 to 10 inches across the southern valley, an example from the region that includes {county} County.

An NWS Morristown study of supercells over the eastern Tennessee River Valley says the topography of the Great Tennessee Valley may have enhanced the pooling of moisture across central east Tennessee. It also says the higher elevations of the northern Cumberland Plateau appeared to influence the development of some tornadoes by enhancing an outflow boundary. The study covers East Tennessee, where {county} County is located.

Davidson.roofing:
What NOAA recorded across Davidson County

Start with hail. For May 2016 through November 2025, the NOAA Storm Events Database holds 69 hail reports filed on 32 separate days in Davidson County. The biggest stones come from May 10, 2016: a 2.50-inch report whose narrative describes tennis-ball-size hail along Andrew Jackson Parkway in Hermitage, alongside two 1.75-inch NOAA reports from Old Hickory and Tulip Grove that same night. Reports of 1.50 inches are dated March 25, 2021 (filed under Oak Hill, with narratives naming Green Hills and the corner of Brightwood Avenue and Lombardy Avenue), January 12, 2023 (near Oak Hill) and March 31, 2023 (Bull Run, in a narrative about a storm east of Ashland City). Sorted by month, 54 of those 69 NOAA reports and 23 of the 32 days land between March and June. May alone holds 25 reports on 8 days; July holds one.

Wind fills the file faster. NOAA lists 431 thunderstorm wind reports on 126 days between April 2016 and April 2026, and 107 of those days fall from March through August. June (90 reports) and July (87) are the two heaviest months. The busiest single date in that NOAA record is July 1, 2023 with 25 reports, followed by July 8, 2016 with 20 and June 15, 2016 with 17. The top estimated gust in the NOAA file, 74 knots, appears twice. One is March 25, 2021, filed under Nashville and described as a microburst 6 miles long and half a mile wide, running from the Napier area through East Nashville and Inglewood. The other is December 11, 2021, filed under Maplewood, where the narrative gives a straight-line wind swath about 2 miles long in Madison between Briley Parkway at Gallatin Pike and Neelys Bend Road.

Tornado entries arrive in clusters. NOAA lists 18 tornado reports on 9 days from March 2017 through April 2026: five of them on December 11, 2021 and two each on August 31, 2017, November 18, 2017, June 21, 2019, May 4, 2021 and December 9, 2023. The March 3, 2020 entry is rated EF3, and its narrative has the track starting west of River Road Pike, crossing Bells Bend and the Cumberland River near John C. Tune Airport, then running more than 60 miles east through Wilson and Smith counties. The December 9, 2023 Madison entry is rated EF2 and begins just east of I-24. The Bordeaux (August 31, 2017), Joelton (November 18, 2017) and Forest Grove (April 28, 2026) entries are rated EF1. The December 11, 2021 narratives name paths near Cub Creek Road, on Martingale Drive in Old Hickory, near Cooks Landing Court and Stewarts Ferry Pike, and near the Stones River at I-40 in Hermitage; no rating is given for them here because NOAA's rating field and narrative text differ on several of those entries. The 2026 file used here is the one NOAA created on September 18, 2026; NOAA says it updates the current year's file each month, so the 2026 counts can change. These entries describe weather across Davidson County. None is a record of a particular home, and none forecasts a future storm.

Housing stock

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year table DP04) counts 357,113 housing units in Davidson County. Of the 324,907 occupied units, 171,526 (52.8 percent) are owner-occupied and 153,381 are renter-occupied. The same table sorts all units by building type: 176,279 (49.4 percent) are 1-unit detached, 32,704 are 1-unit attached, and 68,742 (19.2 percent) sit in buildings of 20 or more units. By year built, the survey's median is 1986. The 2020 to 2024 survey puts 21,631 units at 1939 or earlier and 76,368 (21.4 percent) at 2010 or later. Adding every band through 1979 in that survey gives 146,507 units, or 41.0 percent. As a general observation, an older home may already have had its first replacement.

Permits and local rules

Permits come from the Metro Nashville Department of Codes and Building Safety, whose pages give 615-862-6500 and a counter at 800 President Ronald Reagan Way, 1st Floor, open Monday through Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Its Residential Building Permits page, updated October 31, 2025, lists "Install siding, roofing, fireplaces or solar panels" among the times a building permit is required, and it describes "repairs to an existing roof not to exceed 33 percent of the roof area" as normal maintenance repairs. The department's renovation page, updated January 17, 2025, has a table headed "Required for 1 and 2 Dwellings." There, "Roofing, New Layer or Replacing More Than 1/3 of The Roof" is marked Yes. So is a carpentry row that includes "Roof Decking More Than 64 Sq. Ft.," while "Gutters, Downspouts" is marked No. Confirm with the department whether your own re-roof needs a permit before work starts.

On that renovation page, the applicant sends a Residential Permit Application to the Zoning Help Desk and lists the work in its Scope of Work section. After zoning review the applicant gets a checklist of other signoffs, and the page says "It is your responsibility to follow the requirements of the checklist." It adds that it is "the applicant's responsibility to schedule the necessary inspections with Metro Nashville at the proper time in the building process."

An owner who occupies or intends to occupy a single-family residence may take out a "Self Permit," with notarized affidavits, and then "the property owner assumes all responsibility" for meeting the codes. If a house is held in an LLC or trust, the renovation page limits a self-permit to work under $25,000. The same page tells owners to check Parcel Viewer for overlays, and for a property in the Neighborhood Conservation Overlay or the Historic Preservation Overlay to "contact the Historic Commission to inquire about any relevant regulations." The pages we read publish no rule on roof layers or ice barrier, so check with the department.

To look up past permits, the Property Permit History page says to open the Parcel Viewer map, search the address and "select Permit History."

On Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors pages read in early October 2026, Davidson is second in the board's list of nine Home Improvement counties, where the license "is required for residential remodeling projects from $3,000 to $24,999." For work of $25,000 or more, the board's contractor page says a contractor license is needed "before contracting, including bidding, offering to engage, or negotiating a price." The Verify a License search on tn.gov shows a license number.

Before you ask for bids on a Davidson County roof

- Your insurer's written estimate, if one exists, so each bid starts from one document.

- A question for each bidder: who pulls the Metro permit, and will the permit number appear in the contract?

- A question about deck work, since the department's table lists roof decking over 64 square feet as a Yes row.

- A Parcel Viewer check for overlays on your parcel.

- Each bidder's Tennessee license number, checked in the Verify a License search.

Shelby.roofing:
Weather reports on file for Shelby County

The hail file for Shelby County is smaller than the wind file, but it has some winter dates. From March 2016 to April 2026, NOAA's Storm Events Database logs 66 hail reports across 32 days. Hail appears in 11 calendar months and never in October. April and May carry 34 of the 66 reports, and May has hail on 9 separate days, more than any other month. The busiest year is 2025, with 17 reports, 10 of them on April 2, 2025. The 2026 file used here is the one NOAA created on September 18, 2026; NOAA says it updates the current year's file each month, so the 2026 counts can change.

The largest stone in that NOAA file is 2.00 inches, logged under Capleville on January 25, 2021, with a narrative reading "Two-inch hail reported on Shelby Drive." On April 2, 2025, NOAA lists a 1.75-inch report from Lenow and another, filed under Collierville ARPK, whose narrative is a Facebook report of golf-ball-size hail near Shelby Drive and Forest Hill Irene Road. Seven NOAA reports from February 2023 through April 2025 give 1.50 inches: Millington (February 15, 2023), Bailey (April 27, 2023, where the narrative puts ping-pong-size hail at Houston Levee Road and Poplar Avenue), White Station (August 9, 2023), Germantown (September 5, 2023), Brunswick (July 8, 2024, along Highway 70 near Lakeland City Hall), Ellendale (March 30, 2025) and Cordova (April 2, 2025).

Thunderstorm wind is the bigger count. Between March 2016 and April 2026, NOAA records 188 thunderstorm wind reports on 77 days, and May, June and July supply 111 of them; July alone has 41. The busiest year in that NOAA record is 2023, with 55 reports, including 10 on June 25 and 7 each on July 18 and July 21. Earlier, May 27, 2017 produced 10 reports under labels such as West Union, Frayser, Cordova and Berclair. The top estimated gust in the file is 78 knots at Raleigh on March 9, 2017, in a narrative that sets the scene near the old Raleigh Springs Mall. A 74-knot report at Memphis International Airport on March 31, 2023 comes with a narrative about straight-line winds across southern and southeast Shelby County that evening. Another 18 NOAA entries are filed as High Wind or Strong Wind; two of them quote Memphis International Airport gusts of 55 mph on March 25, 2024 and 58 mph on September 1, 2024.

NOAA's file for January 2016 through April 2026 holds a single tornado report for the county: an EF1 on October 21, 2019, which began at Memphis International Airport and lifted in the Balmoral area of East Memphis. These are weather entries for the whole county. None describes a specific house, and none predicts a coming storm.

Housing in Shelby County

For the 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year table DP04), the Census Bureau counts 404,333 housing units in Shelby County and 362,741 occupied ones. Owners live in 196,379 of the occupied units (54.1 percent) and renters in 166,362. Single-family detached houses make up 268,206 units (66.3 percent) of that survey's total, buildings of 5 or more units hold 85,732 (21.2 percent) and mobile homes number 4,783. The survey's median year built is 1977. In that survey the largest single year-built band is 1970 to 1979 at 64,689 units, and only 4,361 units date from 2020 or later. Every band through 1979 adds up to 220,208 units, or 54.5 percent. As a general observation, an older home in the county may already have had its first roof replacement.

Permits and licenses for a roof replacement

Memphis and Shelby County Construction Enforcement, on develop901.com, says it reviews plans, issues construction permits and inspects projects in "Memphis, Arlington, Germantown, Lakeland, Millington, and unincorporated Shelby County." Bartlett and Collierville are not on that list, so a home there should check with its own town. Its Policy for Roof Installations, revised June 8, 2022, answers the reroof question for a single-family home: "No, a permit is not required unless the decking is to be repaired or altered." It adds that "New sheathing or repair to sheathing does require a permit," and that because reroofs need no permit, "we may never see the work that was done."

The policy sets Chapter 9 of the 2021 International Residential Code as the standard, with no amendment "other than we do not require an ice barrier." It answers "Yes" on underlayment and on a drip edge. For existing decking, it allows gaps up to an average of 1/4 inch; beyond that, the gaps must be filled or the deck overlaid with 3/8-inch structural panel sheathing, and an overlay "will require a letter from a structural engineer." Where a code violation is brought to the office's attention, the policy says "we will cite the owner of the property." On how many roof layers a house may have, it says the answer depends on site-specific circumstances and the materials used, and it points the reader to the building code, so ask the office.

The policy also defines three terms. A roof repair is "reconstruction or renewal of any part of an existing roof," recovering is installing "an additional roof covering over a prepared existing roof covering without removing the existing roof covering," and replacement is removing the covering, repairing "any damaged substrate" and installing a new one.

For permit records, the Construction Enforcement page offers a permit activity search that lets you "Search and download permits and associated documents for submitted applications." Its questions and answers say a homeowner may make improvements to a single-family dwelling under TCA section 62-6-103 when the home is not for resale, rent or lease, and that a statement of ownership letter is needed before the permit issues. A separate answer says Tennessee-licensed contractors register that license with Construction Enforcement, which asks for a registration fee and a surety bond except for work regulated by the State Alarm Board, and it gives the Licensing Section's number, 901-222-8390.

The roof policy asks whether a Tennessee license is required for roofing in Shelby County and answers "Yes, when a project is over $3,000." The Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors pages, read in early October 2026, give two tiers: a Home Improvement license for residential remodeling "from $3,000 to $24,999" in nine counties, Shelby being the last one listed, and a contractor license "for projects of $25,000 or more." The Verify a License search on tn.gov looks up a number.

Before you ask for bids on a Shelby County roof

- Your insurer's estimate, if you have one, kept at hand for every bidder to read.

- A question for each bidder about underlayment and drip edge, which the county policy says it enforces.

- A question for each bidder: will the job involve deck repair or new sheathing, and who pulls the permit if it does?

- The license number for each bidder, searched in Verify a License, plus the bidder's registration with Construction Enforcement.

Knox.roofing:
Knox County in NOAA's archive

Hail is the thin part of Knox County's record, and it is lumpy. The Storm Events Database lists 42 hail reports on 19 days between May 2016 and October 2025. Spring brings 18 of them: April and May, spread over 6 days. Then comes a September surprise, 9 reports squeezed into September 4, 2025, the heaviest single hail day in the county's record. Counted by year, 2025 leads with 16 reports on 3 days (April 10 with 6, September 4 with 9, October 21 with 1). The latest entry we pulled is dated May 20, 2026. The 2026 file used here is the one NOAA created on September 18, 2026; NOAA says it updates the current year's file each month, so the 2026 counts can change.

Seven NOAA hail reports reach 1.75 inches, the top size for 2016 through 2025. The places are Farragut on May 2, 2016, where the narrative says golf-ball-size hail; near Clinton Highway and Schaad Road at Powell on March 21, 2017; West Knoxville on April 22, 2017, with a narrative adding "several locations in the surrounding vicinity"; Millertown on May 26, 2024; Solway and Robinson on April 10, 2025; and Beaver Ridge on September 4, 2025. Smaller 1.50-inch reports include Virtue, three miles west of Farragut, on the same day as the Farragut report in 2016, and Lovell on July 14, 2016.

Wind entries outnumber hail entries by more than four to one: 182 thunderstorm wind reports on 94 days between February 2016 and May 2026, according to NOAA. July (37) and August (34) lead the months, and May through August total 127 reports on 66 days. The busiest year in the NOAA record is 2023 with 31 reports, led by August 12, 2023 with 7. May 26, 2024 stands out for pairing 6 wind reports with the Millertown hail. Five reports at 61 knots on March 29, 2020, filed between 4:46 and 5:09 a.m. Eastern Standard Time under Cowards, Blue Grass, Farragut, South Knoxville and Lake Forest, come with radar-estimated times in three of their NOAA narratives. Other 61-knot entries are Copper Ridge (June 21, 2021, with radar-estimated winds near 70 mph and trees down across north Knox County), Beverly (July 30, 2024), Norwood (May 20, 2025) and Sequoyah Hills (December 18, 2025). The peak, 63 knots, was read from a home anemometer at Lovell on May 20, 2025, and May 20, 2026 closes the data with 5 more reports.

Seven more NOAA entries use the High Wind or Strong Wind labels. A 52-knot High Wind entry for September 27, 2024 cites about 100 Knox 911 calls for fallen trees during the Helene wind event, and a December 29, 2024 entry says the McGhee Tyson weather station recorded gusts above 40 mph for several hours, peaking at 51 mph at 12:49 p.m.

NOAA lists one tornado report between 2016 and May 2026, an EF2 on August 7, 2023 near Byrds Chapel. Its narrative has the tornado starting on Yarnell Road and reaching its peak width as it passed the Lovell Crossing apartment complex. Every entry above is a weather report for the county as a whole. None points to a particular home, and none forecasts a future storm.

Housing stock

Table DP04 of the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year) gives Knox County 218,661 housing units, 201,146 of them occupied. Homeowners live in 131,117 of the occupied units (65.2 percent); renters live in 70,029. By building type, 144,045 units (65.9 percent) are single-unit detached homes, 43,404 (19.8 percent) are in buildings of 5 or more units, and 7,792 (3.6 percent) are mobile homes. The survey puts median construction at 1985, with 2000 to 2009 the biggest single band (32,892 units), just ahead of 1990 to 1999 (32,641). Adding every band up to 1979 in that survey gives 94,524 units (43.2 percent), and 14,943 (6.8 percent) go back to 1939 or earlier. A general observation, not a statistic: where housing is older, more roofs have already been through one replacement.

Permits and local rules for a re-roof

The City of Knoxville's Plans Review and Inspections office, at 400 Main Street, Suite 475, is the city's permit office. Its Plans Review and Permits page lists residential permit types that include Residential Alteration/Repair, and its Fast Fact Guides page, which lists 17 guides including Residential Permit Requirements and Third-Party Inspections for IRC Residential Projects, gives a general rule that one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses need a construction permit unless the work is exempt under section R105.2 of the residential code. The city's Construction Codes page lists the 2024 International Residential Code. The same guides page, in its section on state design rules, says "A qualified registrant is required for roof replacements or reroofs of all buildings of 5,000 square feet or more or greater than two stories in height," and it exempts one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses from needing a registered architect or engineer. The pages we read do not say in plain words whether a re-roof of a house needs a permit, and they state no layer limit or ice barrier rule, so check with Plans Review and Inspections (865-215-4311) before work starts.

The Plans Review and Inspections page on knoxvilletn.gov has quick links for Permit Search, Inspection Scheduling, a Daily Inspections List and "Renew or Register to Pull a Permit."

Knox County Codes Administration sits in Suite 547 of the City County Building at the same 400 Main Street address, with a help line at 865-215-2325 and hours listed as Monday through Friday, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm. Its page directs applicants to the Knox Permit Portal and offers a Permit Inspection Lookup for inspection results and scheduled inspections. Its download list includes a Homeowner Permit Affidavit, an Affidavit of Exemption, a Schedule of Fees and a Third-Party Inspection Policy. The page does not say which addresses fall under it, so check with Knox County Codes Administration if your home may be outside the city limits.

The state layer comes from the Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, whose pages were read in early October 2026. Knox is fifth in its list of nine counties where residential remodeling from $3,000 up to less than $25,000 falls under a Home Improvement license, and roofing is named among the improvements. At the top end, the board's contractor page puts the threshold at "projects of $25,000 or more." tn.gov's Verify a License search is the place to check a number.

Before you ask for bids on a Knox County roof

- The insurer's written estimate, when one exists, saved for each bidder.

- Whether your building is a one- or two-family home or a townhouse, because the registrant rule above exempts those.

- The answer to which office handles your address: the city, the Town of Farragut or Knox County Codes Administration.

- Three answers from each bidder: who holds the permit, the permit number, and the Tennessee license number.

Hamilton.roofing:
NOAA's record for Hamilton County

Hail first. The Storm Events Database files 19 hail reports under Hamilton County across 11 dates, the earliest March 1, 2017 and the latest May 12, 2025, and nothing at all for 2016, 2018, 2019, 2020 or 2021. All but one measure an inch or more across. Two sit at the top, 1.75 inches: a March 1, 2017 report labeled Chickamauga, whose narrative says "Golf ball sized hail was reported at Chattanooga." The other is a June 25, 2023 report labeled Brainerd. Three more come in at 1.25 inches, labeled Salem (March 21, 2017), Rathburn (April 10, 2025) and Montlake (May 12, 2025). Eighteen of the 19 fall between March and June, with May leading at 7 reports on 3 dates. The year 2025 supplies 11 reports on 5 dates, and May 2 of that year, with 4 reports, is the single heaviest date.

The wind record is larger. Between June 15, 2016 and June 22, 2026, NOAA files 135 thunderstorm wind reports under Hamilton County on 78 dates; an instrument stands behind 8 of them and an estimate behind the other 127. Every month shows up except October. June leads with 38 reports on 16 dates, then July with 23 on 16 dates, then May with 21 on 12, while March through August together account for 120 reports on 69 dates. Three dates are level at 6 reports apiece: June 20, 2019, June 7, 2025 and June 22, 2026.

The top estimate is 78 knots, labeled White Oak, on June 7, 2025. Its narrative reads "Several large trees snapped at their trunks on Mountain Creek Road by potent thunderstorm wind gusts." Two 70-knot estimates share that date, labeled Ooltewah and Collegedale Arpk. For the second, the narrative reports branches "up to 10 inches in diameter" torn off by the wind and firefighters sent to a home where a branch was "damaging the porch roof of the home." The highest instrument reading is 59 knots on August 7, 2023, filed under the airport station label "(CHA)Lovell Fld Chat". A NOAA label points to a nearby place or station. It is not a street address.

Outside the thunderstorm count, the file has one High Wind entry and one Strong Wind entry for Hamilton. The High Wind entry, September 11, 2017, estimates 50 knots and says "Several trees and power lines were reported down across the county." The Strong Wind entry, December 23, 2022, lists a measured 37 knots and says "A wind gust to 43 mph was measured at the KCHA ASOS."

The tornado side of the file holds two entries. An EF0 dated March 2, 2023 and labeled New Pt to Georgetown covers 2.12 miles and, per its narrative, "lifted just over the Meigs County line". The other is an EF3 dated April 12, 2020, stamped 10:19 p.m. EST and spanning 12.75 miles between the labels East Ridge and Collegedale Arpk. Its narrative opens on the south side of Fort Oglethorpe in Catoosa County, runs across the Tennessee and Georgia state line toward East Brainerd Road, reaches Ooltewah, and "eventually dissipated in southwestern Bradley County."

Reading the dates. Dates follow NOAA's records; its format guide says times are "usually in LST" (local standard time), and every Hamilton County row counted here is stamped EST. During daylight time a stamp therefore trails the wall clock by an hour: 10:19 p.m. EST on April 12, 2020 was 11:19 p.m. EDT on the wall. Two Hamilton wind entries, stamped 11:20 p.m. EST on July 8, 2016 and 11:00 p.m. EST on May 22, 2020, would land on July 9 and May 23 by a wall clock. The 2026 file is preliminary, and NOAA's README says the current year is refreshed monthly. This is a weather record for the county as a whole and says nothing about any one house or any coming storm.

The county's homes

The Census Bureau's American Community Survey for 2020 to 2024 (5-year table DP04) reports 168,013 housing units in Hamilton County, of which 154,181 are occupied and 13,832 vacant (8.2 percent). Owners hold 98,531 of the occupied units (63.9 percent) and renters 55,650 (36.1 percent). By structure type, 114,261 units (68.0 percent) are detached single-family houses, 6,781 are attached, 8,399 (5.0 percent) are in two-unit buildings, 16,050 (9.6 percent) are in buildings of 20 or more units and 5,247 (3.1 percent) are mobile homes.

On age, table B25035 puts the median year built at 1982. Back in DP04, 14,419 units (8.6 percent) date to 1939 or earlier, and the bands through the 1970s add up to 80,935 units, or 48.2 percent of the stock. Another 48,560 units (28.9 percent) were built in 2000 or later. The table cannot tell you when your own roof went on, so look for that date in your paperwork.

Offices, permits and licenses

Where your address sits decides who answers the permit question. Hamilton County's Building Inspection Department, 4005 Cromwell Road in Chattanooga, 423-209-7860, open 8:00 A.M. to 4:00 P.M. Eastern, states "A building permit is required for any new, alteration, addition or repair to a structure." The exceptions it lists (storage buildings, fences, finish work like painting and carpeting, and similar items) leave roofing out. Its page also carries a directory of inspection offices for Chattanooga, Collegedale, East Ridge, Lakesite, Red Bank, Signal Mountain, Soddy-Daisy and Lookout Mountain, prefaced by "Inspections and forms may change depending on where your building is located." Ridgeside and Walden do not issue their own construction permits, so those addresses use the county's forms.

Inside Chattanooga, the Land Development Office's Residential Modification Permit page names the job outright. The permit is for "modifications to existing structures that don't alter the footprint", covering single-family units where there is a remodel of the interior, "replacing an existing deck, repairing a porch, re-roofing, windows, exterior doors, or siding replacement." Applying means logging in to the city's online permit portal, and the page lists 423-643-5894. It sets out no contractor-license rule, so ask the office who may apply.

Two Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors pages, read in October 2026, set the state's dollar bands. The Home Improvement page reads "A Home Improvement license is required for residential remodeling projects from $3,000 to $24,999", limited to counties that adopted the law, and Hamilton is third of the nine it names; the page counts roofing as home improvement work. At the top band, the contractor page ties a license to "projects of $25,000 or more". It links a Verify a License search that was not used for this page, so that lookup is yours to run.

Before you collect bids on a Hamilton County roof

- The written estimate from your insurer, if you have one, so every bidder starts from the same sheet.

- Which office serves your address: Chattanooga, one of the other towns on the county's list, or the county department.

- For each bidder, a plain question: who files the permit, and will its number be written into the contract?

- Which band your contract total falls in, $3,000 to $24,999 or $25,000 and up, because the Board's pages treat them differently.

- The Tennessee license number each bidder gives you, looked up in the Board's Verify a License search.

Rutherford.roofing:
Rutherford County in NOAA's files

Begin with the hail table. For Rutherford County, NOAA's Storm Events Database holds 36 hail reports on 22 dates between June 3, 2016 and May 20, 2025, with no report for 2019 or 2020. Twenty-seven of them are an inch or larger, spread over 17 dates, and ten reach an inch and a half or more, over 7 dates. Two are logged at 2.00 inches. The first, May 6, 2024, is labeled Christiana and described as "Estimated 1.5 to 2 inch hail". The second, March 30, 2025, is labeled La Vergne, and its narrative says "Estimated 2 inch hail was reported between Nolensville and Smyrna." Next down are two at 1.75 inches: the May 26, 2024 report labeled Murfreesboro ("Golf ball size hail was reported west of Murfreesboro") and the May 20, 2025 report labeled Eagleville ("Estimated golf ball size hail was reported near Christiana from a tornado-warned thunderstorm"). March through June account for 30 of the 36 reports and 18 of the 22 dates; May has 14 reports on 7 dates, and four reports come from July. Four reports on May 26, 2024 make that the busiest hail date.

For thunderstorm wind, the file lists 138 reports on 64 dates from March 31, 2016 through June 9, 2026, with an instrument behind 8 and an estimate behind 130. By month: June has 32 reports on 11 dates, March 26 on 9, July 20 on 11 and August 19 on 9. March 21, 2017 and August 13, 2019 share the top spot with 9 reports each.

The 78-knot estimates all come from May 8, 2024: four entries, two labeled Pleasant Hill and two labeled Mt Vernon, sharing one narrative about straight line winds near Eagleville. In it a National Weather Service survey finds "peak winds up to 90 mph" bringing down trees along Highway 99, Taylor Road and Jackson Ridge Road, and notes that "Several homes and outbuildings also suffered roof damage." Another entry, 74 knots on June 21, 2019 and labeled Jefferson Spgs, has a narrative tracing a downburst from I-840 near Hickory Grove Road over Mona Road and Powells Chapel Road to around Walterhill. The top instrument reading, 71 knots on March 1, 2017 and labeled Hales Camp, comes with the line "The roof was blown off and doors blown out of a hangar at the Smyrna Airport" and a gust that NOAA's narrative calls "unofficial". Airport stations supply the next readings: 58 knots on April 13, 2022 at Smyrna, then two of 53 knots, one on May 3, 2020 (labeled Sewart AFB, with a narrative about the Smyrna Airport) and one on June 17, 2022 at Murfreesboro.

Winds filed to a forecast zone, with no thunderstorm behind them, are 1 High Wind and 7 Strong Wind entries. The High Wind entry, March 3, 2023, measures 52 knots and cites a Smyrna airport station that "measured a peak non-thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph." The seven Strong Wind entries are on seven different dates, April 5, 2017 through March 15, 2026, four of them in April. One, January 12, 2024, says "Strong winds in downtown Murfreesboro near the square downed a tree onto a garage."

Eleven tornado entries land on 9 dates from March 1, 2017 to March 15, 2025, and several are only the Rutherford segment of a path that began in another county. On March 25, 2021 an EF1 of 2.23 miles crossed western Smyrna; its narrative says it "moved northeast through a residential area along Rock Springs Road" and that "Dozens of houses sustained minor to moderate roof damage in 3 different neighborhoods." April 1, 2023 has three entries, EF1, EF1 and EF2. The EF2, 12.4 miles between the labels Rucker and Kittrell, is placed "six miles south of downtown Murfreesboro near County Farm Road", then northeast along Elam Road, with peak winds estimated at 130 mph. An EF0 on July 29, 2024 began just east of Memorial Boulevard and ended southeast of Middle Tennessee State University on Copper Hollow Drive, with winds estimated at 75 mph. The EF2 of November 6, 2018 covers 8.55 miles between the labels Newtown and Plainview.

How to read the clock. Dates follow NOAA's records; its format guide says times are "usually in LST" (local standard time), and every Rutherford County row counted here is stamped CST. A stamp made during daylight time therefore sits an hour behind a wall clock in CDT. The La Vergne hail entry, stamped 11:05 p.m. CST on March 30, 2025, was already March 31 on a wall clock. NOAA's 2026 data is still preliminary, and its README says the current year's file gets updated every month. Everything above describes weather across the county, not any one property, and none of it predicts what comes next.

Who lives here, and in what

According to the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year table DP04), Rutherford County has 138,929 housing units. Occupied units number 129,431 and vacant ones 9,498 (6.8 percent). Owners occupy 83,895 units (64.8 percent) and renters 45,536 (35.2 percent). Detached single-family houses total 93,739 (67.5 percent) and attached ones 9,693 (7.0 percent); buildings of 3 or 4 units hold 3,796 (2.7 percent), buildings of 20 or more hold 10,217 (7.4 percent) and mobile homes number 3,386 (2.4 percent).

Table B25035 gives a median year built of 2001. Only 2,365 units (1.7 percent) go back to 1939 or earlier, and the bands through the 1970s sum to 26,023 units, or 18.7 percent. Construction since 2000 totals 71,542 units (51.5 percent), among them 30,025 (21.6 percent) from the 2010s. None of this dates an individual roof, so find your own installation date.

Codes offices and the state license

Rutherford County and the City of Murfreesboro each run a codes office, and Smyrna, La Vergne and Eagleville, which came up above, may answer for their own addresses; this page did not read their permit pages. The county Building Codes Department, 1 South Public Square, Room 101, 615-898-7734, covers re-roofing in its Building Code FAQ. The FAQ gives the hours as Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. Central, and says the office "closes promptly" at 4:15 p.m. Central. Asked "Am I required to obtain a permit to re-roof my house?", it answers "A building permit is not required only if re-roofing or covering does not require the replacement and/or repairs of roof sheathing, rafters or support beams." On layers, it answers "Two." and says that when the second layer is replaced "both layers of old roofing should be removed prior to installing new roofing."

The Murfreesboro Building and Codes Department, 111 West Vine Street, 615-893-3750, Monday through Friday 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Central, has an FAQ stating "A permit is required in order to construct, alter, convert, repair, enlarge, move or demolish any building or structure or part thereof". A second answer places "minor repairs to chimneys, porches, underpinning or roofing" among "normal maintenance repairs" that need no permit. It never says whether a complete replacement counts as minor, so check with the department. For the Historic Zoning District, it tells homeowners to call the Murfreesboro Planning Department at 615-893-6441 before exterior renovations.

On the state side, Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors pages read in October 2026 say Home Improvement licensing applies "to the counties adopting the law", list Rutherford eighth of nine, and define home improvement to cover "roofing". The Board's contractor page ties a state license to "projects of $25,000 or more". The Board's pages link a Verify a License search, which was not used for this page, so run the lookup yourself.

Lining up before bids come in

- Any written estimate from your insurer, kept where each bidder can read it.

- Whether your property is in Murfreesboro or under the county department, since each posts its own permit answers.

- A question for every bidder: if the job needs sheathing, rafter or support-beam work, who applies for the permit?

- A count of the shingle layers on the roof today, and a plan for what comes off.

- Each bidder's Tennessee license number, checked in the Verify a License search.

Williamson County: what the NOAA file shows

Hail first. NOAA's Storm Events Database logs 99 hail reports on 29 dates by NOAA's clock in Williamson County, from May 1, 2016 through November 7, 2025. Of those, 83 reports on 20 dates are an inch or larger, and 17 reports on 7 dates are two inches or larger. Three are filed at 3.00 inches. On May 26, 2024 the Leipers Fork entry says "Three inch hail was reported in the Leipers Fork area. Many vehicles sustained damage due to broken windows and car dents." On May 20, 2025, an entry labeled Douglas puts "Estimated 3-inch hail" on Keystone Drive south of Franklin, and one labeled Peytonsville says "Measured 3-inch hail was reported in Franklin." A 2.75-inch entry the same day, labeled Franklin, reads "Estimated baseball size hail was reported near Franklin." That date has 25 hail reports, the largest tally for any single date in this county's file; May 26, 2024 has 11 and March 27, 2021 has 8, with 2.25 inches at College Grove the largest that day. May is the leading month at 49 reports on 7 dates, and March through June together hold 84 reports on 20 dates. Looking by year, 2025 has 43 reports on 6 dates, 2024 has 18 on 3 and 2021 has 13 on 3.

Thunderstorm wind spans April 6, 2016 to April 28, 2026: 209 reports on 83 dates, 4 tied to an instrument and 205 to an estimate. June has 47 reports on 17 dates, July has 33 on 12, March has 30 on 11 and April has 25 on 9. July 8, 2016 tops the dates with 13 reports and September 10, 2016 follows with 12.

For strength, the file's top estimate is 74 knots on June 19, 2019, labeled Calle. The narrative sketches a microburst "approximately 3.2 mile long by 1 mile wide" across northeastern Thompson's Station and northern Spring Hill, with "minor roof and exterior damage" to some buildings. Two 70-knot estimates share March 1, 2017. The Mallorys entry describes a downburst that snapped or uprooted trees on Crossroads Boulevard and Mallory Lane near the Cool Springs Galleria, with winds "estimated around 80 mph." The La Vergne entry runs a narrative across northeast Williamson, southeast Davidson and northwest Rutherford counties, a reminder that a NOAA label does not pin an entry to a single place. For measured gusts, the highest is 60 knots on December 11, 2021, labeled Mallorys, where a home weather station "measured a wind gust of 69 mph."

Two entries filed to a forecast zone are High Wind, and five on 4 dates are Strong Wind. May 4, 2020 estimates 52 knots and reports "Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in Fairview, Franklin, Nolensville, and Brentwood with several roads blocked." March 3, 2023 estimates 50 knots and lists "roof and other property damage across all of Williamson County." On May 1, 2017, two Strong Wind entries name a tree on Crescent Centre Drive in Cool Springs and a split tree on Clovercroft Road.

Six tornado entries fall on six dates, March 1, 2017 through March 30, 2025. The EF1 of March 1, 2017 covers 10.48 miles between the labels Berrys Chapel and Nolensville. Its narrative has it touching down "along Hillsboro Road just northwest of the city of Franklin," crossing "the Cool Springs and Brentwood areas of northern Williamson County" and lifting just west of the Davidson County line. An EF0 on August 12, 2023 touches down 1.2 miles northeast of downtown Franklin and lifts near Highway 96 at Royal Oaks Boulevard, with winds estimated at 75 mph. The four other entries, February 6, 2019, September 1, 2020, May 9, 2021 and March 30, 2025, are all EF0; the 2019 entry is the Williamson piece of a path from Dickson County and the 2025 entry continues one from Hickman County.

On timestamps. Dates follow NOAA's records; its format guide says times are "usually in LST" (local standard time), and every Williamson County row counted here is stamped CST. That is one hour off the wall clock while daylight time is in force. The Nolensville hail entry ("Estimated 2 inch hail was reported southwest of Nolensville") shows the effect: stamped 11:00 p.m. CST on March 30, 2025, it would read March 31 on a wall clock, so the 29 hail dates above are NOAA's count by NOAA's clock and a local clock would make it 30. Because 2026 data is preliminary and NOAA's README says current-year files are refreshed monthly, a later download of the 2026 file may differ. Nothing here describes a particular house or predicts a storm.

Housing in the county

Census Bureau figures for 2020 to 2024 (American Community Survey 5-year table DP04) put Williamson County at 96,921 housing units: 92,214 lived in and 4,707 empty (4.9 percent). Households that own number 72,671 (78.8 percent), and households that rent number 19,543 (21.2 percent). Single-family detached houses account for 75,214 units, or 77.6 percent. Another 5,294 are attached houses, 7,374 (7.6 percent) are units in buildings of 20 or more, and 1,457 (1.5 percent) are mobile homes.

Table B25035 gives 2002 as the median year built. Of all units, 2,184 (2.3 percent) were built in 1939 or earlier and 15,921 (16.4 percent) before 1980, against 51,702 (53.3 percent) built since 2000, 25,689 of those (26.5 percent) in the 2010s. These are county-wide counts; they cannot say when any particular roof was installed.

Permit offices and state licensing

More than one office answers for roofs in Williamson County, and the address decides which. For the unincorporated county, Williamson County Building Codes, 1320 West Main Street, Suite 400, Franklin, 615-790-5718, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm Central, posts a memo dated August 1, 2025, "Code Requirements for Roof Repair or Replacement". The memo states "a building permit and inspection is not required for residential roof repairs or replacements", then adds that the work "shall comply with adopted codes and ordinances, including Chapter 9/Roof Assemblies of the 2021 IRC" and that materials "shall be installed in accordance with the manufacturer's installation instructions."

In the City of Franklin, the Building and Neighborhood Services Department states "A building permit is required for all new construction, additions, renovations, decks, pools and most repair work" and gives 615-794-7012 for questions about whether a project needs one. The Franklin department's hours are 7:30am to 5:00pm Central, Monday through Friday. The page does not name roofing, so put the question to the department before assuming either way. An applicant whose property lies in a Historic Preservation Overlay must contact the Historic Preservation Planner in the Planning and Sustainability Department before any construction permit is issued. The page lets a homeowner pull a permit, and in the page's own words, "If the cost of the work exceeds $25,000 a State of Tennessee licensed contractor must pull the permit." Brentwood, Fairview, Nolensville and Thompson's Station also appear above; this page did not read their permit pages, so ask the office that serves your address.

Tennessee's licensing pages split by county. The Board for Licensing Contractors' Home Improvement page, read in October 2026, applies to counties that adopted the law and lists nine: Bradley, Davidson, Hamilton, Haywood, Knox, Marion, Robertson, Rutherford and Shelby. Williamson is absent from that list. Above that tier, the Board's contractor page ties a state license to prime-contractor work of $25,000 or more, and says the license is needed before "bidding, offering to engage, or negotiating a price". A Verify a License search is linked from the Board's pages; it was not run for this page, so run it yourself before relying on any license number.

Before you request bids in Williamson County

- A written estimate from your insurer, if you hold one, saved where each bidder can see it.

- Your address: inside the City of Franklin, inside another town, or in the unincorporated county.

- A question for each bidder about who applies for a permit, if one is needed, and whether its number goes into the contract.

- A question about the manufacturer's installation instructions, which the county memo mentions.

- A check of whether the contract total is under $25,000 or at $25,000 or more, then the license number each bidder gives you, looked up in the Verify a License search.
